1   Introduction  Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states   h t , as a function of the previous hidden state   h t − 1   and the input for position   t . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.  2   Background  The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence- aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].  3   Model Architecture  Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations   ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to a sequence of continuous representations   z   = ( z 1 , ..., z n ) .   Given   z , the decoder then generates an output sequence   ( y 1 , ..., y m )   of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. 2

Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position- wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is  LayerNorm( x   + Sublayer( x )) , where   Sublayer( x )   is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension   d model   = 512 .  Decoder:   The decoder is also composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position   i   can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than   i .  3.2   Attention  An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors. This allows every position in the decoder to attend over all positions in the input sequence. This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models such as [38, 2, 9]. • The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder. Each position in the encoder can attend to all positions in the previous layer of the encoder. • Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata. One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types. As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires   O ( n )   sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence 6

length   n   is smaller than the representation dimensionality   d , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size   r   in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to   O ( n/r ) . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work. A single convolutional layer with kernel width   k < n   does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of   O ( n/k )   convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or   O ( log k ( n ))   in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of   k . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to   O ( k   ·   n   ·   d   +   n   ·   d 2 ) . Even with   k   =   n , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model. As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models. We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix. Sentences were encoded using byte-pair encoding [3], which has a shared source- target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. For English-French, we used the significantly larger WMT 2014 English-French dataset consisting of 36M sentences and split tokens into a 32000 word-piece vocabulary [38]. Sentence pairs were batched together by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.  5.2   Hardware and Schedule  We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. In contrast to RNN sequence-to-sequence models [37], the Transformer outperforms the Berkeley- Parser [29] even when training only on the WSJ training set of 40K sentences.  7   Conclusion  In this work, we presented the Transformer, the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, replacing the recurrent layers most commonly used in encoder-decoder architectures with multi-headed self-attention. For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers.   On both WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks, we achieve a new state of the art. In the former task our best model outperforms even all previously reported ensembles. We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video. Making generation less sequential is another research goals of ours. The code we used to train and evaluate our models is available at   https://github.com/ tensorflow/tensor2tensor . 1   Introduction  Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states   h t , as a function of the previous hidden state   h t − 1   and the input for position   t . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.  2   Background  The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence- aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].  3   Model Architecture  Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations   ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to a sequence of continuous representations   z   = ( z 1 , ..., z n ) .   Given   z , the decoder then generates an output sequence   ( y 1 , ..., y m )   of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. 2

Figure 1: The Transformer - model architecture. The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder, shown in the left and right halves of Figure 1, respectively.  3.1   Encoder and Decoder Stacks Encoder:   The encoder is composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position- wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is  LayerNorm( x   + Sublayer( x )) , where   Sublayer( x )   is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension   d model   = 512 .  Decoder:   The decoder is also composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position   i   can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than   i .  3.2   Attention  An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors. The output is computed as a weighted sum 3

The input consists of queries and keys of dimension   d k , and values of dimension   d v   . We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by   √ d k , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix   Q . The keys and values are also packed together into matrices   K   and   V   . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code. While for small values of   d k   the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of   d k   [3]. This allows every position in the decoder to attend over all positions in the input sequence. This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models such as [38, 2, 9]. • The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder. Each position in the encoder can attend to all positions in the previous layer of the encoder. • Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. The positional encodings have the same dimension   d model  as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed. There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9]. That is, each dimension of the positional encoding corresponds to a sinusoid. The wavelengths form a geometric progression from   2 π   to   10000   ·   2 π . We chose this function because we hypothesized it would allow the model to easily learn to attend by relative positions, since for any fixed offset   k ,   P E pos + k   can be represented as a linear function of  P E pos . We also experimented with using learned positional embeddings [9] instead, and found that the two versions produced nearly identical results (see Table 3 row (E)). We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.  4   Why Self-Attention  In this section we compare various aspects of self-attention layers to the recurrent and convolu- tional layers commonly used for mapping one variable-length sequence of symbol representations  ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to another sequence of equal length   ( z 1 , ..., z n ) , with   x i , z i   ∈   R d , such as a hidden layer in a typical sequence transduction encoder or decoder. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata. One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types. As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires   O ( n )   sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence 6

length   n   is smaller than the representation dimensionality   d , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size   r   in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to   O ( n/r ) . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work. A single convolutional layer with kernel width   k < n   does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of   O ( n/k )   convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or   O ( log k ( n ))   in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of   k . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to   O ( k   ·   n   ·   d   +   n   ·   d 2 ) . Even with   k   =   n , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model. As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models. We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix. Not only do individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many appear to exhibit behavior related to the syntactic and semantic structure of the sentences.  5   Training  This section describes the training regime for our models.  5.1   Training Data and Batching  We trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset consisting of about 4.5 million sentence pairs. Sentences were encoded using byte-pair encoding [3], which has a shared source- target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. For English-French, we used the significantly larger WMT 2014 English-French dataset consisting of 36M sentences and split tokens into a 32000 word-piece vocabulary [38]. Sentence pairs were batched together by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.  5.2   Hardware and Schedule  We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. For our base models using the hyperparameters described throughout the paper, each training step took about 0.4 seconds. We trained the base models for a total of 100,000 steps or 12 hours. For our big models,(described on the bottom line of table 3), step time was 1.0 seconds. The big models were trained for 300,000 steps (3.5 days).  5.3   Optimizer  We used the Adam optimizer [20] with   β 1   = 0 . 9 ,   β 2   = 0 . 98   and   ϵ   = 10 − 9 . For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers.   On both WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks, we achieve a new state of the art. In the former task our best model outperforms even all previously reported ensembles. We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video. 1   Introduction  Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states   h t , as a function of the previous hidden state   h t − 1   and the input for position   t . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.  2   Background  The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence- aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].  3   Model Architecture  Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations   ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to a sequence of continuous representations   z   = ( z 1 , ..., z n ) .   Given   z , the decoder then generates an output sequence   ( y 1 , ..., y m )   of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. 2

The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder, shown in the left and right halves of Figure 1, respectively.  3.1   Encoder and Decoder Stacks Encoder:   The encoder is composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position- wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is  LayerNorm( x   + Sublayer( x )) , where   Sublayer( x )   is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension   d model   = 512 .  Decoder:   The decoder is also composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position   i   can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than   i .  3.2   Attention  An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors. The input consists of queries and keys of dimension   d k , and values of dimension   d v   . We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by   √ d k , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix   Q . The keys and values are also packed together into matrices   K   and   V   . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code. While for small values of   d k   the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of   d k   [3]. This allows every position in the decoder to attend over all positions in the input sequence. This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models such as [38, 2, 9]. • The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder. Each position in the encoder can attend to all positions in the previous layer of the encoder. • Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to   −∞ ) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata. One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types. As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires   O ( n )   sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence 6

length   n   is smaller than the representation dimensionality   d , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size   r   in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to   O ( n/r ) . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work. A single convolutional layer with kernel width   k < n   does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of   O ( n/k )   convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or   O ( log k ( n ))   in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of   k . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to   O ( k   ·   n   ·   d   +   n   ·   d 2 ) . Even with   k   =   n , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model. As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models. We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix. Not only do individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many appear to exhibit behavior related to the syntactic and semantic structure of the sentences.  5   Training  This section describes the training regime for our models.  5.1   Training Data and Batching  We trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset consisting of about 4.5 million sentence pairs. Sentences were encoded using byte-pair encoding [3], which has a shared source- target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. For English-French, we used the significantly larger WMT 2014 English-French dataset consisting of 36M sentences and split tokens into a 32000 word-piece vocabulary [38]. Sentence pairs were batched together by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.  5.2   Hardware and Schedule  We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. For our base models using the hyperparameters described throughout the paper, each training step took about 0.4 seconds. We trained the base models for a total of 100,000 steps or 12 hours. 1   Introduction  Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states   h t , as a function of the previous hidden state   h t − 1   and the input for position   t . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.  2   Background  The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence- aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].  3   Model Architecture  Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations   ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to a sequence of continuous representations   z   = ( z 1 , ..., z n ) .   Given   z , the decoder then generates an output sequence   ( y 1 , ..., y m )   of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. 2

Figure 1: The Transformer - model architecture. The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder, shown in the left and right halves of Figure 1, respectively.  3.1   Encoder and Decoder Stacks Encoder:   The encoder is composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position- wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is  LayerNorm( x   + Sublayer( x )) , where   Sublayer( x )   is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension   d model   = 512 .  Decoder:   The decoder is also composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position   i   can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than   i .  3.2   Attention  An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors. The output is computed as a weighted sum 3

The input consists of queries and keys of dimension   d k , and values of dimension   d v   . We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by   √ d k , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix   Q . The keys and values are also packed together into matrices   K   and   V   . Dot-product attention is identical to our algorithm, except for the scaling factor of   1 √ d k  . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code. While for small values of   d k   the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of   d k   [3]. This allows every position in the decoder to attend over all positions in the input sequence. This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models such as [38, 2, 9]. • The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder. Each position in the encoder can attend to all positions in the previous layer of the encoder. • Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. We implement this inside of scaled dot-product attention by masking out (setting to   −∞ ) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections. See Figure 2.  3.3   Position-wise Feed-Forward Networks  In addition to attention sub-layers, each of the layers in our encoder and decoder contains a fully connected feed-forward network, which is applied to each position separately and identically. We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.  4   Why Self-Attention  In this section we compare various aspects of self-attention layers to the recurrent and convolu- tional layers commonly used for mapping one variable-length sequence of symbol representations  ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to another sequence of equal length   ( z 1 , ..., z n ) , with   x i , z i   ∈   R d , such as a hidden layer in a typical sequence transduction encoder or decoder. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata. One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types. As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires   O ( n )   sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence 6

length   n   is smaller than the representation dimensionality   d , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size   r   in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to   O ( n/r ) . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work. A single convolutional layer with kernel width   k < n   does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of   O ( n/k )   convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or   O ( log k ( n ))   in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of   k . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to   O ( k   ·   n   ·   d   +   n   ·   d 2 ) . Even with   k   =   n , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model. As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models. We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix. Not only do individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many appear to exhibit behavior related to the syntactic and semantic structure of the sentences.  5   Training  This section describes the training regime for our models.  5.1   Training Data and Batching  We trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset consisting of about 4.5 million sentence pairs. Sentences were encoded using byte-pair encoding [3], which has a shared source- target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. For English-French, we used the significantly larger WMT 2014 English-French dataset consisting of 36M sentences and split tokens into a 32000 word-piece vocabulary [38]. Sentence pairs were batched together by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.  5.2   Hardware and Schedule  We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. For translation tasks, the Transformer can be trained significantly faster than architectures based on recurrent or convolutional layers.   On both WMT 2014 English-to-German and WMT 2014 English-to-French translation tasks, we achieve a new state of the art. In the former task our best model outperforms even all previously reported ensembles. We are excited about the future of attention-based models and plan to apply them to other tasks. We plan to extend the Transformer to problems involving input and output modalities other than text and to investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms to efficiently handle large inputs and outputs such as images, audio and video. 1   Introduction  Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states   h t , as a function of the previous hidden state   h t − 1   and the input for position   t . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.  2   Background  The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence- aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].  3   Model Architecture  Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations   ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to a sequence of continuous representations   z   = ( z 1 , ..., z n ) .   Given   z , the decoder then generates an output sequence   ( y 1 , ..., y m )   of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. 2

The Transformer follows this overall architecture using stacked self-attention and point-wise, fully connected layers for both the encoder and decoder, shown in the left and right halves of Figure 1, respectively.  3.1   Encoder and Decoder Stacks Encoder:   The encoder is composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. Each layer has two sub-layers. The first is a multi-head self-attention mechanism, and the second is a simple, position- wise fully connected feed-forward network. We employ a residual connection [11] around each of the two sub-layers, followed by layer normalization [1]. That is, the output of each sub-layer is  LayerNorm( x   + Sublayer( x )) , where   Sublayer( x )   is the function implemented by the sub-layer itself. To facilitate these residual connections, all sub-layers in the model, as well as the embedding layers, produce outputs of dimension   d model   = 512 .  Decoder:   The decoder is also composed of a stack of   N   = 6   identical layers. In addition to the two sub-layers in each encoder layer, the decoder inserts a third sub-layer, which performs multi-head attention over the output of the encoder stack. Similar to the encoder, we employ residual connections around each of the sub-layers, followed by layer normalization. We also modify the self-attention sub-layer in the decoder stack to prevent positions from attending to subsequent positions. This masking, combined with fact that the output embeddings are offset by one position, ensures that the predictions for position   i   can depend only on the known outputs at positions less than   i .  3.2   Attention  An attention function can be described as mapping a query and a set of key-value pairs to an output, where the query, keys, values, and output are all vectors. The output is computed as a weighted sum 3

The input consists of queries and keys of dimension   d k , and values of dimension   d v   . We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by   √ d k , and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix   Q . The keys and values are also packed together into matrices   K   and   V   . Additive attention computes the compatibility function using a feed-forward network with a single hidden layer. While the two are similar in theoretical complexity, dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code. While for small values of   d k   the two mechanisms perform similarly, additive attention outperforms dot product attention without scaling for larger values of   d k   [3]. This allows every position in the decoder to attend over all positions in the input sequence. This mimics the typical encoder-decoder attention mechanisms in sequence-to-sequence models such as [38, 2, 9]. • The encoder contains self-attention layers. In a self-attention layer all of the keys, values and queries come from the same place, in this case, the output of the previous layer in the encoder. Each position in the encoder can attend to all positions in the previous layer of the encoder. • Similarly, self-attention layers in the decoder allow each position in the decoder to attend to all positions in the decoder up to and including that position. We need to prevent leftward information flow in the decoder to preserve the auto-regressive property. We chose the sinusoidal version because it may allow the model to extrapolate to sequence lengths longer than the ones encountered during training.  4   Why Self-Attention  In this section we compare various aspects of self-attention layers to the recurrent and convolu- tional layers commonly used for mapping one variable-length sequence of symbol representations  ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to another sequence of equal length   ( z 1 , ..., z n ) , with   x i , z i   ∈   R d , such as a hidden layer in a typical sequence transduction encoder or decoder. Motivating our use of self-attention we consider three desiderata. One is the total computational complexity per layer. Another is the amount of computation that can be parallelized, as measured by the minimum number of sequential operations required. The third is the path length between long-range dependencies in the network. Learning long-range dependencies is a key challenge in many sequence transduction tasks. One key factor affecting the ability to learn such dependencies is the length of the paths forward and backward signals have to traverse in the network. The shorter these paths between any combination of positions in the input and output sequences, the easier it is to learn long-range dependencies [12]. Hence we also compare the maximum path length between any two input and output positions in networks composed of the different layer types. As noted in Table 1, a self-attention layer connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas a recurrent layer requires   O ( n )   sequential operations. In terms of computational complexity, self-attention layers are faster than recurrent layers when the sequence 6

length   n   is smaller than the representation dimensionality   d , which is most often the case with sentence representations used by state-of-the-art models in machine translations, such as word-piece [38] and byte-pair [31] representations. To improve computational performance for tasks involving very long sequences, self-attention could be restricted to considering only a neighborhood of size   r   in the input sequence centered around the respective output position. This would increase the maximum path length to   O ( n/r ) . We plan to investigate this approach further in future work. A single convolutional layer with kernel width   k < n   does not connect all pairs of input and output positions. Doing so requires a stack of   O ( n/k )   convolutional layers in the case of contiguous kernels, or   O ( log k ( n ))   in the case of dilated convolutions [18], increasing the length of the longest paths between any two positions in the network. Convolutional layers are generally more expensive than recurrent layers, by a factor of   k . Separable convolutions [6], however, decrease the complexity considerably, to   O ( k   ·   n   ·   d   +   n   ·   d 2 ) . Even with   k   =   n , however, the complexity of a separable convolution is equal to the combination of a self-attention layer and a point-wise feed-forward layer, the approach we take in our model. As side benefit, self-attention could yield more interpretable models. We inspect attention distributions from our models and present and discuss examples in the appendix. Not only do individual attention heads clearly learn to perform different tasks, many appear to exhibit behavior related to the syntactic and semantic structure of the sentences.  5   Training  This section describes the training regime for our models.  5.1   Training Data and Batching  We trained on the standard WMT 2014 English-German dataset consisting of about 4.5 million sentence pairs. Sentences were encoded using byte-pair encoding [3], which has a shared source- target vocabulary of about 37000 tokens. For English-French, we used the significantly larger WMT 2014 English-French dataset consisting of 36M sentences and split tokens into a 32000 word-piece vocabulary [38]. Sentence pairs were batched together by approximate sequence length. Each training batch contained a set of sentence pairs containing approximately 25000 source tokens and 25000 target tokens.  5.2   Hardware and Schedule  We trained our models on one machine with 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. nodes.title: Transformer: модель последовательностей, основанная только на механизме внимания
nodes.description: Статья предлагает новый подход к обработке последовательностей без рекуррентных и сверточных слоёв. Главная идея — строить зависимости между токенами только через attention.

nodes.title: Проблема старых моделей: рекуррентность делает обучение последовательным и медленным
nodes.description: RNN, LSTM и GRU долго считались стандартом для перевода и языкового моделирования. Их ключевой недостаток — вычисления идут по позициям последовательно, что мешает параллелизации.

nodes.title: Решение авторов: убрать recurrence и convolutions, оставить self-attention
nodes.description: Transformer заменяет традиционные блоки на многоголовое self-attention и позиционно-независимые feed-forward слои. Это позволяет моделировать дальние зависимости без последовательного прохода по времени.

nodes.title: Преимущества Transformer: выше качество, больше параллелизм, меньше время обучения
nodes.description: Модель показывает лучшую или сопоставимую точность на переводе при значительно меньших затратах на обучение. Дополнительный плюс — архитектура проще и лучше масштабируется на GPU.

nodes.title: Архитектура encoder-decoder: вход кодируется, выход генерируется авто-регрессивно
nodes.description: Как и в классических системах перевода, входная последовательность сначала преобразуется в скрытые представления, а затем декодер генерирует выход по одному токену. Каждый следующий токен зависит только от уже известных предыдущих.

nodes.title: Encoder stack: 6 одинаковых слоёв с self-attention и feed-forward сетью
nodes.description: Энкодер состоит из шести повторяющихся блоков. В каждом блоке сначала идёт multi-head self-attention, затем позиционно-независимая полносвязная сеть.

nodes.title: Decoder stack: 6 слоёв, masked self-attention и attention к encoder output
nodes.description: Декодер тоже имеет шесть слоёв, но дополнительно включает attention к выходу энкодера. Self-attention в декодере маскируется, чтобы не смотреть на будущие позиции.

nodes.title: Residual connection + LayerNorm: стабилизация обучения каждого подслоя
nodes.description: Каждый подслой оборачивается residual-связью и нормализацией. Формула LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x)) помогает сохранять градиент и ускоряет оптимизацию.

nodes.title: Размерность модели d_model = 512: единый формат для всех подслоёв
nodes.description: Все подслои и embedding-слои работают в пространстве размерности 512. Это упрощает сложение представлений и делает архитектуру согласованной.

nodes.title: Scaled dot-product attention: softmax по QKᵀ, делённому на √d_k
nodes.description: Внимание вычисляется как взвешенная сумма значений, где веса зависят от совместимости query и key. Масштабирование на √d_k предотвращает слишком большие значения и проблемы с градиентами.

nodes.title: Формула внимания: Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V
nodes.description: Запись показывает, как матрицы запросов, ключей и значений превращаются в выход attention. Это центральная математическая операция всей модели.

nodes.title: Почему scaling нужен: большие d_k делают dot products слишком крупными
nodes.description: Без деления на √d_k скалярные произведения растут по дисперсии вместе с размерностью. Тогда softmax входит в насыщение, и обучение становится хуже.

nodes.title: Multi-head attention: несколько attention-голов работают параллельно
nodes.description: Вместо одного attention с полной размерностью модель использует несколько проекций в разные подпространства. Затем результаты объединяются и снова проецируются в итоговое представление.

nodes.title: В Transformer используется 8 голов, каждая с d_k=d_v=64
nodes.description: Авторы выбрали восемь параллельных голов, чтобы сохранить вычислительную стоимость примерно на уровне single-head. Маленькая размерность каждой головы компенсируется их количеством.

nodes.title: Три применения attention: encoder-decoder, encoder self-attention, decoder self-attention
nodes.description: Одна и та же идея внимания используется в трёх местах модели. Это делает архитектуру универсальной и позволяет связывать вход, выход и внутренние представления.

nodes.title: Encoder-decoder attention: декодер смотрит на все позиции входа
nodes.description: В этом режиме query берутся из декодера, а keys/values — из энкодера. Так каждая позиция выхода может учитывать всю входную последовательность.

nodes.title: Encoder self-attention: каждая позиция видит все позиции предыдущего слоя
nodes.description: Self-attention в энкодере связывает токены одной и той же последовательности. Это позволяет строить контекстные представления без рекуррентного прохода.

nodes.title: Decoder self-attention: маска запрещает смотреть на будущие токены
nodes.description: Чтобы сохранить авто-регрессивность, декодер не может использовать информацию справа от текущей позиции. Маскирование ставит запрещённые связи в −∞ перед softmax.

nodes.title: Position-wise feed-forward network: две линейные трансформации с ReLU
nodes.description: После attention в каждом слое идёт одинаковая для всех позиций MLP-блок. Он обрабатывает каждый токен отдельно, но с общими параметрами внутри слоя.

nodes.title: FFN размерности: вход и выход 512, скрытый слой 2048
nodes.description: Промежуточное расширение до 2048 увеличивает выразительность нелинейного преобразования. Затем размерность снова возвращается к 512 для совместимости с остальной сетью.

nodes.title: Embeddings и softmax: токены переводятся в векторы и обратно в вероятности
nodes.description: Модель использует обучаемые embedding-матрицы для входа и линейный слой с softmax для предсказания следующего токена. Весовая матрица между embedding и выходом частично разделяется.

nodes.title: Связанные веса embedding и pre-softmax слоя уменьшают число параметров
nodes.description: Одна и та же матрица используется для входных эмбеддингов и финального линейного преобразования. Это упрощает обучение и улучшает согласованность представлений.

nodes.title: Positional encoding: добавляет информацию о порядке без recurrence и convolution
nodes.description: Поскольку Transformer не имеет встроенного механизма порядка, позиционная информация вводится отдельно. Она суммируется с embedding на входе энкодера и декодера.

nodes.title: Синусоидальные positional encodings: sin и cos разных частот
nodes.description: Каждая координата позиционного вектора кодируется синусом или косинусом. Частоты образуют геометрическую прогрессию, что помогает модели различать как близкие, так и дальние позиции.

nodes.title: Преимущество синусоид: можно экстраполировать на более длинные последовательности
nodes.description: Авторы предпочли фиксированные синусоиды обучаемым позиционным векторам. Такой выбор потенциально позволяет работать с длинами, которых не было в обучении.

nodes.title: Почему self-attention выгоден: короткий путь между любыми позициями
nodes.description: Self-attention соединяет все токены за один шаг, поэтому дальние зависимости легче изучать. Это особенно важно для задач перевода и синтаксического анализа.

nodes.title: Сравнение сложности: self-attention, RNN и convolution имеют разные ограничения
nodes.description: Self-attention требует O(1) последовательных операций, тогда как RNN — O(n). Свёртки уменьшают последовательность лучше, чем RNN, но всё равно хуже связывают дальние позиции.

nodes.title: Таблица сравнения: self-attention быстрее при n меньше d
nodes.description: Для типичных sentence representations длина последовательности часто меньше размерности представления. В этом режиме self-attention оказывается вычислительно выгоднее рекуррентных слоёв.

nodes.title: Ограниченный self-attention может ускорить обработку очень длинных последовательностей
nodes.description: Если attention смотреть только на локальное окно размера r, вычисления становятся дешевле. Цена — увеличение максимального пути между позициями до O(n/r).

nodes.title: Интерпретируемость attention: разные головы учатся разным синтаксическим задачам
nodes.description: Авторы показывают, что отдельные головы часто фокусируются на разных типах зависимостей. Это делает модель не только эффективной, но и частично объяснимой.

nodes.title: Обучающие данные: WMT 2014 English-German и English-French
nodes.description: Для перевода использовались стандартные большие корпуса WMT. Англо-немецкий набор содержит около 4.5 млн пар предложений, а англо-французский — около 36 млн.

nodes.title: Токенизация: BPE для EN-DE и word-piece для EN-FR
nodes.description: Для английско-немецкого перевода применяли byte-pair encoding с общим словарём около 37 тысяч токенов. Для английско-французского использовали word-piece словарь примерно на 32 тысячи.

nodes.title: Батчинг по длине: в одном батче примерно 25K source и 25K target токенов
nodes.description: Примеры группировались по приблизительной длине последовательности, чтобы эффективнее использовать память GPU. Это уменьшало паддинг и повышало производительность обучения.

nodes.title: Аппаратная конфигурация: 8 NVIDIA P100 GPU, base за 12 часов, big за 3.5 дня
nodes.description: Базовые модели обучались примерно 100 тысяч шагов, а большие — 300 тысяч шагов. Авторы подчёркивают, что время обучения значительно меньше, чем у конкурентов.

nodes.title: Оптимизатор Adam с warmup и обратным корнем после разогрева
nodes.description: Использовался Adam с β1=0.9, β2=0.98 и очень малым ε. Learning rate сначала линейно растёт 4000 шагов, а затем убывает как inverse square root.

nodes.title: Регуляризация: dropout на подслоях и label smoothing
nodes.description: Dropout применяется к выходам подслоёв и к сумме embedding с positional encoding. Label smoothing снижает переуверенность модели и улучшает BLEU.

nodes.title: Результаты перевода: Transformer превосходит предыдущие SOTA по BLEU
nodes.description: На WMT 2014 модель достигает новых лучших результатов при меньших вычислительных затратах. Это главный эмпирический аргумент в пользу архитектуры.

nodes.title: EN-DE: big model получает 28.4 BLEU и обгоняет лучшие ансамбли
nodes.description: На английско-немецком переводе большая версия Transformer улучшает лучший предыдущий результат более чем на 2 BLEU. Обучение заняло 3.5 дня на 8 GPU.

nodes.title: EN-FR: big model достигает 41.8 BLEU при меньшей стоимости обучения
nodes.description: На английско-французском переводе модель устанавливает новый single-model state of the art. Авторы подчёркивают, что стоимость обучения составляет лишь небольшую долю от прежних лучших систем.

nodes.title: Base model тоже сильный: превосходит многие опубликованные системы
nodes.description: Даже базовая конфигурация Transformer показывает результаты выше многих предыдущих моделей и ансамблей. Это демонстрирует, что выигрыш не зависит только от масштабирования.

nodes.title: Ablation study: проверка важности числа голов, размеров и dropout
nodes.description: Авторы варьируют архитектуру, чтобы понять вклад каждого компонента. Эксперименты показывают, что качество чувствительно к размеру модели и регуляризации.

nodes.title: Меньше d_k ухудшает качество: compatibility через dot product не идеален
nodes.description: При уменьшении размера ключей и запросов BLEU падает. Это намекает, что более сложная функция совместимости может быть полезнее простого скалярного произведения.

nodes.title: Большие модели лучше, а dropout помогает бороться с переобучением
nodes.description: Увеличение глубины и ширины обычно улучшает результаты. Dropout заметно повышает обобщающую способность и стабилизирует обучение.

nodes.title: Learned positional embeddings почти не отличаются от синусоидальных
nodes.description: В одной из абляций авторы заменяют синусоиды обучаемыми позиционными векторами. Результаты оказываются почти одинаковыми, но синусоиды сохраняют преимущество экстраполяции.

nodes.title: Обобщение на constituency parsing: Transformer работает и вне перевода
nodes.description: Чтобы проверить универсальность, модель применили к синтаксическому разбору английских предложений. Задача сложнее из-за длинного выхода и структурных ограничений.

nodes.title: Parsing на WSJ: 4-layer Transformer показывает сильные F1 результаты
nodes.description: На Penn Treebank модель обучали как только на WSJ, так и в semi-supervised режиме. Она достигла результатов, сравнимых или лучших по сравнению со многими предыдущими парсерами.

nodes.title: Semi-supervised parsing: Transformer достигает 92.7 F1 на WSJ 23
nodes.description: При использовании дополнительных корпусов качество ещё выше, чем в режиме только на WSJ. Это подтверждает, что архитектура хорошо переносится на другие NLP-задачи.

nodes.title: Заключение: attention-based модели заменяют рекуррентные архитектуры в sequence transduction
nodes.description: Авторы формулируют Transformer как первый полностью attention-based подход к последовательностям. Они ожидают дальнейшее расширение модели на другие модальности и задачи.

nodes.title: Будущие направления: локальное attention, изображения, аудио, видео и менее последовательная генерация
nodes.description: В конце статьи авторы предлагают исследовать ограниченное внимание для больших входов и выходов. Также они хотят применять Transformer не только к тексту, но и к другим типам данных.

1   Introduction  Recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory [13] and gated recurrent [7] neural networks in particular, have been firmly established as state of the art approaches in sequence modeling and transduction problems such as language modeling and machine translation [35, 2, 5]. Numerous efforts have since continued to push the boundaries of recurrent language models and encoder-decoder architectures [38, 24, 15]. Recurrent models typically factor computation along the symbol positions of the input and output sequences. Aligning the positions to steps in computation time, they generate a sequence of hidden states   h t , as a function of the previous hidden state   h t − 1   and the input for position   t . This inherently sequential nature precludes parallelization within training examples, which becomes critical at longer sequence lengths, as memory constraints limit batching across examples. Recent work has achieved significant improvements in computational efficiency through factorization tricks [21] and conditional computation [32], while also improving model performance in case of the latter. The fundamental constraint of sequential computation, however, remains. Attention mechanisms have become an integral part of compelling sequence modeling and transduc- tion models in various tasks, allowing modeling of dependencies without regard to their distance in the input or output sequences [2, 19]. In all but a few cases [27], however, such attention mechanisms are used in conjunction with a recurrent network. In this work we propose the Transformer, a model architecture eschewing recurrence and instead relying entirely on an attention mechanism to draw global dependencies between input and output. The Transformer allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach a new state of the art in translation quality after being trained for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.  2   Background  The goal of reducing sequential computation also forms the foundation of the Extended Neural GPU [16], ByteNet [18] and ConvS2S [9], all of which use convolutional neural networks as basic building block, computing hidden representations in parallel for all input and output positions. In these models, the number of operations required to relate signals from two arbitrary input or output positions grows in the distance between positions, linearly for ConvS2S and logarithmically for ByteNet. This makes it more difficult to learn dependencies between distant positions [12]. In the Transformer this is reduced to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution due to averaging attention-weighted positions, an effect we counteract with Multi-Head Attention as described in section 3.2. Self-attention, sometimes called intra-attention is an attention mechanism relating different positions of a single sequence in order to compute a representation of the sequence. Self-attention has been used successfully in a variety of tasks including reading comprehension, abstractive summarization, textual entailment and learning task-independent sentence representations [4, 27, 28, 22]. End-to-end memory networks are based on a recurrent attention mechanism instead of sequence- aligned recurrence and have been shown to perform well on simple-language question answering and language modeling tasks [34]. To the best of our knowledge, however, the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention to compute representations of its input and output without using sequence- aligned RNNs or convolution. In the following sections, we will describe the Transformer, motivate self-attention and discuss its advantages over models such as [17, 18] and [9].  3   Model Architecture  Most competitive neural sequence transduction models have an encoder-decoder structure [5, 2, 35]. Here, the encoder maps an input sequence of symbol representations   ( x 1 , ..., x n )   to a sequence of continuous representations   z   = ( z 1 , ..., z n ) .   Given   z , the decoder then generates an output sequence   ( y 1 , ..., y m )   of symbols one element at a time. At each step the model is auto-regressive [10], consuming the previously generated symbols as additional input when generating the next. 2
